This presentation narrows the Group 7 CEP project to AO1. The story moves from Avenue Shabu's profit goal to an evidence-based process for identifying repeat-visit opportunities and testing CRM communication.
:::

## Introduction

Our project examines how Avenue Shabu can connect digital marketing, customer experience, POS behavior, revenue, and profitability. This presentation focuses on **AO1**:

> Identify customer segments and retention opportunities to increase profitable repeat visits.

The proposal treats customer-level marketing as a measurement problem as well as a communication problem. A message cannot be evaluated reliably unless visits can be linked to customers and campaign exposure can be documented.

::: notes
The full project includes several analytics objectives. This presentation addresses only AO1 and does not claim to answer the group's advertising, Instagram, review, or promotion objectives.
:::

## Problem statement

::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
**Business context**

- Avenue Shabu wants to increase profit.
- PO1 is to increase profitable repeat-customer revenue through CRM and email/SMS marketing.
- Management needs evidence connecting marketing activity to visits, revenue, and profitability.
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
**AO1 problem**

Toast guest and transaction records may exist, but incomplete or inconsistent email, phone, or account identifiers may prevent reliable customer-level linkage.

**Decision question:** Which customers should receive retention communication, and how will a resulting return visit be measured?
:::
:::::

The problem is therefore not simply to send more promotions. It is to identify valuable and inactive customer segments, understand retention opportunities, and evaluate whether communication supports profitable repeat behavior.

::: notes
Emphasize that the current presentation is a proposal. The available local project materials describe the business problem and the needed data, but they do not establish current customer retention performance.
:::

## One Analytics Objective

**AO1. Identify customer segments and retention opportunities to increase profitable repeat visits (Frank Renn).**

The project source operationalizes this objective as auditing Toast guest data, defining repeat customers, identifying valuable and inactive segments, and recommending measurable email/SMS campaigns to improve retention and revenue.

::: incremental
- Define a repeat customer as a customer with at least two visits during the selected observation window.
- Segment customers using recency, frequency, spending, and available customer-value indicators.
- Recommend and measure retention communications for segments with different needs.
:::

The primary behavioral outcome is repeat visitation within 180 days. Campaign impact should be described as causal only when treatment and comparison groups are designed appropriately.

[The objective connects segmentation to a business outcome: profitable return visits, not engagement metrics alone.]{.fragment .fade-up}

::: notes
The objective has one central outcome—profitable repeat visits. RFM is a practical starting point for segmentation, but it is not itself proof that a segment will respond to a message.
:::

## Importance

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
**Business importance**

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
- Retention can create more sustainable revenue than one-time discounts.
- Targeted communication can reduce irrelevant offers and protect margin.
- Customer-level evidence can improve CRM and email/SMS decisions.
:::
::::

:::: {.column width="50%"}
**Analytical importance**

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
- Customer identifiers determine whether repeat visits can be observed.
- Satisfaction and dining experience may influence retention before CRM does.
- Profitability requires revenue, cost, redemption, and opt-out measures.
:::
::::
:::::::

AO1 matters because an increase in visits is not automatically an increase in profit. The analysis should distinguish high revenue from high contribution, short-term redemption from sustainable retention, and association from campaign lift.

## Literature review

The AO1 literature supports a connected framework rather than a single promotional tactic:

**Customer experience and perceived value → satisfaction and trust → CRM engagement and retention → repeat visits → customer value and profitability**

This framework follows the Group 7 research review. It recognizes that email, SMS, and loyalty communications should support—not replace—food quality, service quality, atmosphere, cleanliness, price-value, and the overall dining experience.

::: notes
The framework is adapted from the AO1 research section in the Group 7 CEP report. It connects consumer behavior theory to the data and measurement decisions in the methods section.
:::

## Existence of well-established consumer behavior theory/models relevant for the project

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Customer experience and value**

- Customer experience occurs across multiple touchpoints and channels (Lemon & Verhoef, 2016).
- Restaurant quality can influence perceived value, satisfaction, trust, and loyalty intentions (Kim & Han, 2008).
- Restaurant customer value can include functional and emotional dimensions (Croitoru et al., 2024).
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**CRM, retention, and segmentation**

- CRM organizes relationship processes and evaluates customer and firm outcomes (Payne & Frow, 2005; Reinartz, Krafft, & Hoyer, 2004).
- Customer value and lifetime value connect customer benefit to firm value (Kumar & Reinartz, 2016).
- Loyalty programs and rewards can affect customer groups differently (Bolton, Kannan, & Bramlett, 2000; Liu, 2007; Park, Chung, & Woo, 2013).
:::
:::::

These models justify using customer experience measures, RFM-style segmentation, retention outcomes, and profitability measures together. They do not justify assuming that every customer should receive the same offer.

## Assessment of the adequateness of the gathered information/data in solving business problems

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Adequate for**

- Building a theoretical foundation for AO1.
- Describing customer experience, CRM, loyalty, retention, and customer value.
- Guiding a survey, Toast data audit, and retention measurement plan.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Not yet adequate for**

- Estimating Avenue Shabu's current satisfaction or retention rate.
- Proving that email, SMS, or loyalty activity caused repeat visits.
- Calculating true customer lifetime profit without cost and margin data.
:::
:::::

The gathered literature is adequate to support the proposed model, but Avenue-specific customer and POS data are still necessary. The data audit should establish coverage, missingness, duplicate records, identifier-match rates, and the available history before the segments are interpreted.

::: notes
This assessment mirrors the AO1 report: the research supports the model, while the current evidence is insufficient to make Avenue-specific performance claims.
:::

## Need for additional analysis to address the said business problems?

::: incremental
1.  Measure current satisfaction with food quality, service, atmosphere, cleanliness, wait time, price-value, emotional experience, trust, and overall satisfaction.
2.  Establish customer-level tracking with phone numbers, email addresses, or membership accounts that can be connected to Toast transactions.
3.  Measure repeat-guest count, second-visit conversion, visit frequency, time between visits, and 30-, 60-, and 90-day retention.
4.  Test thank-you messages, return-visit reminders, birthday offers, loyalty rewards, new-menu announcements, and targeted promotions by segment.
5.  Compare exposed customers with a similar non-exposed group when possible, and evaluate incremental visits, spending, redemption, contribution margin, and customer lifetime value.
:::

The additional analysis would distinguish short-term promotional activity from sustainable retention and would clarify whether an observed relationship is causal or descriptive.

## Methods

The methods combine a data-quality audit, customer-level aggregation, descriptive segmentation, and campaign measurement. The design uses authorized data only and does not infer identity when the available identifiers are insufficient.

::: notes
The methods are intentionally staged. The project should not begin with campaign recommendations before confirming that customers can be identified consistently and that outcomes can be measured.
:::

## Data and Sampling

::::: columns
::: {.column width="54%"}
**Potential sources**

- Toast guest and transaction records
- Visit dates and order totals
- Promotion and campaign identifiers
- Email/SMS permission and opt-out fields
- Customer research on satisfaction and dining experience
:::

::: {.column width="46%"}
**Sampling and units**

- Use a census of all authorized in-scope transactions during the analysis period.
- Use the customer as the segmentation unit.
- Use visits or transactions for behavior summaries.
- Use customer-campaign exposure for campaign evaluation.
:::
:::::

If a campaign comparison is available, retain eligible exposed customers and select a comparable non-exposed group using the same eligibility rules. Report the analysis period, inclusion rules, customer-match rate, and missing-data rate.

## Data wrangling

The proposed workflow is:

::: incremental
1.  Review the Toast schema, reporting period, permissions, and identifier quality.
2.  Standardize dates, timestamps, email values, phone numbers, and customer identifiers.
3.  Flag duplicate transactions, invalid records, refunds, and unusual orders.
4.  Link transactions to customers only when the matching rule is defensible.
5.  Aggregate visits and spending by customer.
6.  Calculate recency, frequency, monetary value, and retention measures.
7.  Create segment labels and preserve a data dictionary and exclusion log.
:::

This workflow creates an audit trail so that a later campaign report can be reproduced when new Toast data are added.

## Sample characteristics

The table below is illustrative because authorized Toast data have not yet been confirmed. It demonstrates the intended customer-level structure and is not evidence about Avenue Shabu's actual customers.

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)

customer_summary <- tibble(
  customer_id = c("A01", "A02", "A03", "A04"),
  visits = c(5, 2, 7, 1),
  spending = c(420, 160, 610, 55),
  segment = c("high-value", "developing", "high-value", "at-risk")
)

customer_summary |>
  kable()
```

The illustration contains `r nrow(customer_summary)` customer records and `r sum(customer_summary$visits)` visits. The production analysis should also report unique customers, transactions, date range, identifier-match rate, missing values, segment counts, and the rule used to define a repeat customer.

## Measures

| Measure | Proposed definition | AO1 use |
|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------|
| Repeat customer | At least two visits in 180 days | Primary outcome |
| Recency | Days since most recent visit | Identify inactive or at-risk customers |
| Frequency | Number of visits in the analysis period | Identify repeat behavior |
| Monetary value | Total or average spending | Prioritize value, not visits alone |
| Second-visit conversion | Share of new guests returning | Evaluate early retention |
| Campaign result | Incremental visits, revenue, margin, and redemption | Evaluate CRM effectiveness |
| Engagement risk | Unsubscribe or opt-out behavior | Protect customer trust |

Revenue should not be labeled profit unless contribution-margin and campaign-cost data are available. Definitions should be finalized before the analysis so that segments and campaign outcomes remain reproducible.

## Analytics Methods

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="50%"}
**Descriptive and segmentation methods**

::: incremental
- Summarize visits, spending, recency, frequency, and identifier coverage.
- Create RFM-style groups such as high-value, developing, at-risk, and inactive.
- Compare cohorts and time periods to describe retention patterns.
:::
::::

:::: {.column width="50%"}
**Campaign evaluation methods**

::: incremental
- Compare exposed and non-exposed customers when a valid comparison exists.
- Track second visits, repeat frequency, revenue, redemption, margin, and opt-outs.
- Treat before-and-after results as descriptive when no control is available.
:::
::::
:::::::

The first deliverable is a validated customer-level summary. The next is a measurable email/SMS test that connects a defined treatment to profitable repeat-visit outcomes.
